—Jesse Crawford (colored), charged with murpering his wife in this county last year, and who made his escape from jail some months since, having been recaptured and lodged in the Valdosta jail, Capt. T. H. Williard, sheriff, went to the latter place last week and returned on Monday with the prisoner in charge.—Crawford is now confined in jail here awaiting trial at the fall term of court.—Madison Recorder.

—The census enumeration in this county is being retaken. It is believed that the present enumeration will reach from 3,000 to 5,000 more than the first enumeration. This, including the slice that was taken from Marion and given to Levy, which contains a population of 1,500 or more, will show as healthy an increase for Marion as any county in the State, with the exception of Orange, which has more than doubled its population.—Ocala Banner.

—Arnold Brimer, a colored farmer residing about one and a half miles west of the town, exhibited some sugar-cane on last Saturday with forty well-matured joints. This cane was produced near Crosby lake, and we don't believe it can be beat anywhere in the State. Brimer is considered a good farmer, and has owned his present farm since 1868. He has plenty of farm stock and makes from three to four bales of long cotton a year, besides abundant provision crops, all the result of honest labor. —Starke Telegraph.

—Dr. W. A. D'Alemberte informs us that he yesterday met an old Floridian who had tried his fortunes in the Lone Star State, had sickened of his bargain and returned again to the Land of Flowers, where he proposes to rest for the remainder of his days. He is now prospecting, and as soon as located will communicate with other families who are also anxious to return to this land of milk and honey. The Texas like the California fever is fast dying out, and people are realizing that when once established there is "no place like home." —Pensacola Advance.

—The following notice, signed by the President of the Board of Health and Mayor of the town, has been handed to the undertakers and grave-diggers of St. Augustine: "It having become known that in one, or perhaps all the cemeteries of this city, the remains of the dead are frequently exhumed, and the people are exposed to contagion and death as a consequence, even in cases where the dead expired from common diseases; but we are now in greater danger from the large number in our grave-yards of those who died of yellow fever; therefore, the Board of Health issue to you this notice of warning, that especial care should be exercised by those whose duties lie in this direction, to carefully guard against opening any grave, or moving the earth at all near any grave, containing the remains of any one who has died of that disease, for a single hair could open upon us at any time that fell destroyer and depopulate our city."

—On the afternoon of Tuesday Deputy Sheriff McCallum and Constable White went over to LaVilla from Jacksonville to make an arrest of Sharper Mitchell, George Green, Straph Yong and Frank Bowie, negroes, on a warrant sworn out by Ben. Alston, charging them with rioting, fighting and assault. Before the arrests could be made a mob of negroes gathered about the place where the parties were, and when McCallum attempted to arrest Bowie, the mob closed in on him, handling both him and White roughly and releasing the prisoner. The officers rushed off after Bowie, who ran off, and were followed by the mob who knocked down McCallum with a club, kicking his face violently. The chase continued, however, and fearing the prisoner would escape McCallum fired at Bowie, striking his leg and disabling him. The Marshal of LaVilla took a hand in the game at this point, and arrested McCallum, the deputy sheriff of the county, for firing his pistol in the street. Bowie escaped, and was taken to his home and put under medical care. Later, arrests were made, and the whole matter will be investigated.

Some time last May a train of cars was wrecked on the mountain not far from Cresson. One of the cars contained a live alligator, that was on its way to the Zoological Garden in Philadelphia. The car that contained the water animal was tucked into a branch of Conemaugh creek, and it was believed that the alligator had been killed under the wreck. But the fact that a few days ago, as a boy named Pennel Sharp was bathing in a deep place in the stream aforesaid was set upon by some ferocious thing in the water, it has been conjectured that it must be the alligator that was in the car that was wrecked last spring. The Altoona Tribune of last Friday tells of it as follows:

Young Sharp and several companions, who had been out shooting woodcock, had gone in the creek to bathe. As Sharp was swimming by himself some distance from the bank his companions suddenly heard him give an agonizing scream and disappear in the water. They saw that he had been caught by some black animal which had one of his legs in its mouth where it was held firmly by a row of cruel white teeth. The animal carried the young man under the water, but re-appeared in a few seconds with Sharp in his jaws. He cried to his companions to shoot, but before a gun could be discharged he was pulled under the water again. A few moments after he rose with the big black beast still clinging to his leg, and struck out for the opposite shore. Again he called upon his companions to shoot, but being afraid of hitting Sharp no one discharged his gun. At last he reached the bank and began climbing up its slippery side, when, guided by a sudden impulse, the animal gave a jerk which tore a great piece from the calf of Sharp's leg and slid with its mouthful of human flesh into the deep water, to re-appear no more. The wounded man was carried home by his companions more dead than alive. His leg was terribly lacerated, and the loss of blood was very severe. It was thought for a while that the limb could be saved, but mortification set in and it was found necessary to amputate it just below the knee. The young man is now getting along very well and will probably recover. People in the vicinity are in a great state of excitement and will not let their children go near the stream, as they are afraid they will be eaten. Almost a constant watch has since been kept on the place by men armed with shot-guns, who are determined to destroy the beast, but as yet it has failed to show itself."

During the past two weeks the editor of the Selinsgrove Times has been expressing his unhappiness over the fact that a colored man in Lewistown was rotten-egged out of town for insulting a white woman on the street. Weirick has fallen into the mistake of men of his class of mind in not distinguishing the differences between offences. He puts the rotten-egging of the man in Lewistown upon the same level with the offence of driving a colored man out of a community in the South. The fact is, there is no similarity in the cases. The man in Lewistown had no right to insult a lady on the street. To do so was an offence to every decent man in the community. There is no natural or legal right under which a man may insult another, or a whole community, and the man who presumes to deliberately insult a community, cannot be classed with a man who in the pursuit of his natural rights, and legal rights, is set upon by a set of ruffians and driven from a community. The class of newspapers to which the Selinsgrove Times belongs, fail to have the discrimination to see that the colored people in the South are not driven out for insult offered to women, but they are driven out because of opinion's sake; for holding opinions that are as wholesome on the questions of morals, religion and politics as are the opinions of the men who drive them out. The Times fails to see the difference in the cases; it fails to see that the man in Lewistown who was egged out of town, was a man dangerous to society generally. That his opinions were of the most pernicious quality, and that his conduct was his opinions put into practice. The truth is, that the fellow that was driven out of Lewistown and the bull dozer of the South are alike, for both by their practice would prevent people from the exercise of natural and legal rights. The man in Lewistown would prevent a lady from walking peaceably on the public streets, and the bull dozer in the South would prevent their opponents from the peaceable exercise of their natural and legal rights on the highway, and in their own houses.

CANADIAN EMIGRATION TO THE UNITED STATES. The United States consul at Port Sasnia, in a dispatch to the Department of State, dated July 27, says that the prosperity, which is so universal throughout the states, is in marked contrast to the general depression which prevails in Canada. The "outs" throw the blame upon Sir John A. MacDonald and his tariff policy for the prevailing state of affairs, while the organs of the party in power repel these accusations. The result, however, would seem to be an exodus from Canada of some of her best citizens. Consul Pace says that the emigrants who crossed over at that point alone during the year ending June 30, 1880, and who declared their intentions of becoming permanent residents of the United States numbered 77,059.

NO COMPROMISE PROBABLE BETWEEN THE FUNDERS AND READJUSTERS.—A Virginia journalist who was in the city to-day said to a STAR reporter that there is no earthly prospect of any compromise between the regular and readjuster wings of the democratic party in that state. The leaders of the regular wing, he said, do not want a compromise, for the reason that they do not believe it would add any strength to the Hancock ticket. Very many of the regular democrats are so violently opposed to making any further concessions to the readjusters that they would refuse to join in a fusion movement, and the ticket would, thereby, lose more support than it could gain from the Mahonites. The STAR's informant said that the managers of the regular democratic canvass believe that more than half of the readjusters will vote the regular Hancock and English ticket, and that this will make the state secure for the democrats.

THE ELECTION IN ALABAMA yesterday were for state officers and members of the legislature, the latter of which will elect a U. S. Senator in the place of Hon. Geo. S. Houston, deceased. For state officers the democrats had a full ticket in the field, headed by Rufus W. Cobb, the present incumbent, for governor. The republicans made no nominations, but were advised by their state committee to support a greenback-labor and independent ticket, headed by James M. Pickens. The legislature last chosen was almost unanimously democratic, the senate being composed of 30 democrats and 80 Republicans.

The legislature last chosen was almost unanimously democratic, the senate being composed of 30 democrats and 2 independents, and the house of representatives of 3 republicans, 91 democrats, 4 independent democrats and 2 nationals, giving the straight-out democrats a clear majority of 110 over all opponents of whatever kind. In 1876, Tilden, for President, had over 34,000 majority, and in 1875, Cobb, for governor, had 88,531 majority. In opposition to the regular democratic ticket yesterday was one made by a fusion ticket of republicans, greenbackers and independents. Verbal reports from election officers at the closing of the polls show a clear majority for the straight-out democratic ticket. Reports at the democratic executive committee rooms from the interior of the state leave no doubt of Alabama poiling a heavy democratic vote. Further returns in Mobile county show a clean sweep for the democrats against the republicans and greenbackers. The lowest candidate will have 1,000 majority. Tuscaloosa, Perry, Dallas, Bullock, Macon and Montgomery counties go heavily democratic. The returns from Madison, Limestone and Morgan are highly favorable. There will be 50,000 majority at least for the state ticket.

The Moss and Russell Affair.
Mr. Spofford, the librarian of congress, is undoubtedly a very valuable officer so far as arranging and cataloguing a vast number of volumes for convenience is concerned, but these high qualifications should not be dimmed by an act of rank injustice, which involves a palpable wrong. Some time since THE REPUBLICAN made bare reference to an affair which occurred in the congressional library between two employees—one a white democrat named Lowell Russell and the other a colored republican named John A. Moss. The facts and circumstances connected with the affair are substantially these: Moss, who is a great admirer of General Garfield, had placed over his desk likenesses of Garfield and Arthur, the republican candidates for president and vice-president. This representation was pulled down by Russell and stamped under his feet on the floor to its ruin. When Moss discovered the outrage he replaced it with another, and soon Russell treated this as he had the former one. Moss then ascertained to his full satisfaction that Russell had destroyed his pictures, and went to him and asked if he had done the act. Russell replied that he had and asked insolently "What do you propose to do about it?" To this insolent remark Moss very promptly and properly replied "I can only say that it was a very cowardly act in you to destroy my property while absent from my desk so that I could not defend it." This was a very truthful remark for the act was one of marked
interposed his authority in a very arbitrary and unjust manner, as appears in the sequel. He at once dismissed Moss, the wronged party, from service and continued Russell for the time, instead of dismissing both, as should have been the case if either was to have been punished. He subsequently gave Russell a leave of absence for the month of July, and it is understood with pay. On the 1st of August Russell, at the end of his leave, returned to duty, while Moss is thrown out of his situation entirely, and without redress. It is said by those conversant with the library that Moss is by far the most efficient and valuable employee of the two, but he is unfortunately a colored republican, while the aggressor is a white democrat. This would indicate the direction of Mr. Spofford's political sympathies at this time, for the rankest democrat would scarcely be guilty of an act of equal injustice under the circumstances. This is the tale briefly and correctly told in accordance with the strict facts of the case. Mr. Spofford was appointed by President Lincoln, at a period when democrats were not honored with civil places under a republican administration, and has hold his position undisturbed through all succeeding republican administrations. Nevertheless he cannot substantiate his worthiness to be retained by the occurrence here narrated. It is very doubtful if rank injustice in the exercise of power can be covered from responsibility by other excellences of official character. No man, no matter how elevated his position, can afford to do a palpable wrong, for sooner or later all wrong must come to judgment.

There has been an increase of over ten million of dollars in the national revenue receipts during the fiscal year just closed.

The Post Office Department has never been self-sustaining. It is gratifying, therefore, to learn that the excess of expenditures over receipts are less the past fiscal year than at any time since 1867.

General Garfield will not be likely to get any Mormon votes, if there are citizens of that faith residing where there are legal voters. He is on the record in the most emphatic manner as an enemy of the poiygamous abominations of Mormonism. In 1879, soon after the decision of the United States Supreme Court in the Reynolds case was given, General Garfield wrote a letter, which is published in the Salt Lake (Utah) Tribune, in which he says:

I rejuse with you that the Supreme Court has rendered more effective the execution of our laws against polygamy. I will remember what you say in case any bill comes up for action at the present session.
